n: After Jerusalem fell, Jeremiah had apparently been swept up with the captives and taken in chains to Ramah, a holding camp north of Jerusalem for deportees. There Nebuzaradan set him free.

f.g: About 5 miles north of Jerusalem; the staging point for the march to Babylon.

n: The Babylonian commander takes Jeremiah aside and says, “The Lord your God announced this disaster on this place.”
“And now he has done what he said, because you people sinned and didn’t obey him.” Strikingly, a pagan officer understands Judah’s fall better than Judah’s leaders did.
“I’m freeing you from your chains today. Come to Babylon if you wish, and I’ll look after you—or stay. The whole land is open to you; go wherever you think best.”

Before Jeremiah could reply, he added: “Go back to Gedaliah, whom Babylon has made governor of Judah, and live with him among the people—or go wherever you like.” He gave him food and a gift and let him go.

f.g: A seal impression reading “belonging to Gedaliah, who is over the house” found at Lachish may refer to him.

n: Jeremiah chose to stay with the poor remnant in the land, going to Gedaliah at Mizpah. He could have had comfort in Babylon but stayed with his people.

f.g: A town in Benjamin, about 8 miles north of Jerusalem, now the administrative center.

n: Army officers and their men still hiding in the countryside heard that Gedaliah had been appointed governor over the remaining poor people—men, women, and children not taken to Babylon.

f.w: the captains of the forces which were in the fields
f.g: Commanders of Judean troops who had escaped the city and were scattered in the countryside.

n: They came to Gedaliah at Mizpah: Ishmael, Johanan and Jonathan sons of Kareah, Seraiah, the sons of Ephai, and Jezaniah, with their men.

f.g: From Netophah, a village near Bethlehem.
From Maacah, a region northeast of Galilee.

n: Gedaliah swore to them: “Don’t be afraid to serve the Babylonians. Settle in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and things will go well.” This was Jeremiah’s own counsel.

f.w: Fear not to serve the Chaldeans

n: Gedaliah would represent them before the Babylonians at Mizpah; meanwhile they should harvest wine, summer fruit, and oil, store it, and live in the towns they had occupied.

f.g: Figs and similar fruits harvested in late summer.

n: Jews who had fled to Moab, Ammon, Edom, and other lands heard that a remnant had been left in Judah under Gedaliah.
They came home to Judah, to Gedaliah at Mizpah, and gathered an abundant harvest. A brief, hopeful season of renewal after catastrophe.

f.w: gathered wine and summer fruits very much

n: Johanan and the other commanders came to Gedaliah at Mizpah with a warning.

“Do you know that Baalis, king of the Ammonites, has sent Ishmael to assassinate you?” But Gedaliah didn’t believe them. Ammon was resisting Babylon and wanted the pro-Babylonian government in Judah gone.

f.w: Baalis the king of the Ammonites
f.g: An Ammonite seal impression mentioning a king named Ba‘alyasha‘ has been found, possibly the same man.

n: Johanan offered secretly to kill Ishmael first: “Why let him kill you, scatter everyone gathered to you, and destroy the remnant of Judah?”
Gedaliah forbade it: “Don’t do this—what you say about Ishmael isn’t true.” His trusting, honorable nature would cost him his life.
